name: Pauxiána
confidence_why: The only two first-hand records of this extinct Cariban language, Meyer 1956 (a short missionary essay that remarks in passing on "frequent paroxytone accentuation" and whose transcription key marks primary and secondary stress) and Salathé 1932 (a wordlist whose accent marks fall on both final and penultimate syllables, e.g. tuná, uató, yutú beside núna, póta, kúita), state no stress rule, and Loukotka 1968, d'Almada 1861 and Fabre 2005 say nothing about stress, so the placement is left undetermined.

catalog_quote: [Meyer 1956 p. 13] As indicações por êle ministradas provaram-me de que a hipótese da língua Pauxiána pertence ao grupo Cariba parece ser a única aceitável e que certas características Arnak. em particular wapixána, como por exemplo a freqüente acentuação paroxítona, demonstram o inverso da outra hipótese, a saber de que a origem Cariba juntou-se a influência Aruak. [p. 31, Acentos e sinais diacríticos] "'" sobre vogal = acento tônico (principal), quando necessário assinala-lo em oposição a outros acentos. ... "á, í, ú" - O acento agudo - ´- sobre as vogais a, i, u, indica sempre a respectiva tonacidade (principal ou secundária). [Salathé 1932 p. 307 key] ', indique l'accent. [p. 308 forms] Tuná: eau. uató: feu. oró: terre. núna: lune. ukomó: gens. urémungú: enfant. irá: champ. yutú: forêt. yónna: nez. póta: bouche. pélămápŏto: barbe. kávas: tabac. káipi: chapeau. rotáina: se baisser. uaipú: ouate. putáiukú: uriner. sorópă: perroquet (Papagei). kúita: perroquet (Sittich). aranatá: guariba. pŏrókomi: canne à sucre.

[p. 13] — Ditongos: Quando, para maior clareza, se torna necessário ou conveniente assinalar o ditongo com acento tónico, terá, o sinal "'" sobre o ditongo v. gr. aú [p. 29]
new_statements.translation: The indications he [Dom Mauro Wirth O.S.B., Wapishana specialist] supplied proved to me that the hypothesis that the Pauxiána language belongs to the Carib group seems the only acceptable one, and that certain Arawak characteristics, in particular Wapishana ones, such as for example the frequent paroxytone (penultimate) accentuation, show the reverse of the other hypothesis, namely that Arawak influence was added to a Carib origin. — Diphthongs: When, for greater clarity, it becomes necessary or convenient to mark a diphthong with the tonic accent, it will carry the sign ' over the diphthong, e.g. aú.
new_statements.citation: Meyer, Alcuino. 1956. Pauxiána: pequeno ensaio sobre a tribo Pauxiána e sua língua, comparada com a língua Macuxí. Rio de Janeiro: Arquivo Nacional (Ministério da Justiça e Negócios Interiores).
new_statements.locator: p. 13 (PDF page 14), section 'A Língua' introduction; diacritics key p. 29 (PDF page 30)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (54 PDF pages, Curt Nimuendajú scan) and rendered printed pp. 13, 29-33 (pp. 14, 30-34) as images. Printed p. 13 (p. 14) carries the quoted sentence exactly as reported: "As indicações por êle ministradas provaram-me de que a hipótese da língua Pauxiána pertence ao grupo Cariba parece ser a única aceitável e que certas características Arnak. em particular wapixána, como por exemplo a freqüente acentuação paroxítona, de-monstram o inverso da outra hipótese, a saber de que a origem Cariba juntou-se a influência Aruak." (only differences: "Arnak." with a stray period mark, and "de-monstram" hyphenated across a line). Printed p. 29 (p. 30) "A Língua - Exemplar da Pronuncia - Sinais Dacrí…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meyer states only a tendency: penultimate (paroxytone) accent is 'frequent' in Pauxiána, which he reads as Arawak (Wapishana) influence on a Cariban language; he gives no placement rule. The only other primary record, Salathé's 1932 accent-marked wordlist (pp. 308-313), shows accent on the final syllable in a large share of items (tuná, uató, oró, ukomó, urémungú, yutú, uaipú, aranatá) as well as on penults (núna, yónna, póta, kávas, káipi, rotáina), so the two records do not converge on a single position: no rule can be extracted, and Meyer's 'frequent penult' sits uneasily with Salathé's oxytone-heavy forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Meyer's 'freqüente' itself implies non-paroxytone words exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated citation forms (wordlists). Meyer's 855-item Portuguese-Pauxiána-Macuxí vocabulary, which presumably carried his accent marks, was left unpublished (p. 28: 'Consta o vocabulário anexo, não publicado, de 55 páginas datilografadas'); only the 50-page essay was printed.
new_statements.identity_note: Meyer 1956 and Salathé 1932 both describe the Pauxiána/Paushiana of the upper Catrimani (Rio Caterimany) and Mucajaí rivers, Roraima — the same variety Glottolog codes paux1236. Not to be confused with Pauxi/Pawiyana (paux1235, a Tiriyó-group language on the Trombetas/Cachorro), which is what Loukotka 1968 lists under 'Pauxi'. Meyer's essay compares Pauxiána with Macuxí and speculates about Wapishana (Arawak) admixture; the accent remark is framed as evidence for that admixture, not as a phonological description in its own right.

sources.note: The only substantial Pauxiána lexicon recorded by a linguist-missionary who worked with the last speakers; Meyer's diacritics key (p. 29) shows he marked the tonic accent, so the typescript would give the accent position for c. 850 words and let the 'frequent paroxytone' claim be checked against Salathé's oxytone-heavy list. Meyer says it exists as an annex; its whereabouts (Arquivo Nacional, Rio; Mosteiro de São Bento; or the Boa Vista Benedictine mission archive) are unknown.
